chapters.title: Persistence, replication, Sentinel, Cluster and Valkey
chapters.summary: How Redis survives restarts and failures and how it scales: RDB vs AOF, async replication, Sentinel failover, Cluster sharding and the Redis/Valkey choice.

lesson.heading: Persistence: RDB and AOF
lesson.body:
Redis is in-memory, but it can persist to disk:

- **RDB snapshots**: a compact point-in-time dump written by a forked child process (copy-on-write), on a schedule (`save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000`) or via `BGSAVE`. Fast restarts and good for backups, but you lose everything since the last snapshot on a crash. Forking a large dataset can briefly stall and temporarily needs extra memory for pages modified during the snapshot.
- **AOF (append-only file)**: logs every write command. `appendfsync everysec` (the default and usual choice) loses at most about a second of writes; `always` fsyncs every write (safest, slowest); `no` leaves it to the OS. The AOF is periodically **rewritten** (compacted) in the background; since Redis 7 it is stored as a base file plus incremental files (multi-part AOF).
- **Both**: the common production setup. With `aof-use-rdb-preamble` (default on) the rewritten AOF starts with an RDB snapshot followed by recent commands, combining fast loading with good durability.
- **None**: valid for a pure cache that can start empty.

Persistence is not a backup strategy by itself: copy RDB files off the machine regularly.

code.source:
# redis.conf
save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000      # RDB: after 1h/1 change, 5m/100 changes, 60s/10k changes
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec
aof-use-rdb-preamble yes

lesson.heading: Replication
lesson.body:
A primary streams its write commands to one or more **replicas** (`REPLICAOF host port`). Replicas serve reads (scaling read throughput) and are failover candidates. Initial sync transfers an RDB snapshot; afterwards the replication stream continues, and short disconnections resume via partial resync from a backlog buffer.

Replication is **asynchronous**: the primary acknowledges writes before replicas have them. Consequences:

- Reads from replicas can be **stale** (replication lag).
- If the primary fails, the most recent acknowledged writes may be **lost** after a replica is promoted.
- `WAIT numreplicas timeout` blocks until writes reach N replicas, reducing (not eliminating) loss windows; `WAITAOF` (Redis 7.2+) waits for AOF fsync locally and/or on replicas.

lesson.heading: High availability with Sentinel
lesson.body:
**Redis Sentinel** provides automatic failover for a primary/replica setup without sharding. Run at least **three** Sentinel processes on separate machines. They monitor the primary; when a **quorum** agrees it is down, they elect a leader Sentinel that promotes a replica, reconfigures the other replicas, and publishes the new primary address.

Clients connect to Sentinels to discover the current primary (ioredis and node-redis support Sentinel configs) and must handle reconnection. Use `min-replicas-to-write` to make the primary refuse writes when it cannot reach enough replicas, limiting split-brain data loss.

lesson.heading: Scaling out with Redis Cluster
lesson.body:
**Redis Cluster** shards data across multiple primaries, each with replicas, and provides failover without Sentinel. The keyspace is split into **16,384 hash slots**; a key's slot is `CRC16(key) mod 16384`, and each primary owns a range of slots.

- Clients are cluster-aware: they cache the slot map and follow **MOVED** (slot permanently moved) and **ASK** (slot migrating) redirects.
- **Multi-key operations** (MGET, MULTI, Lua scripts, SUNION) only work when all keys are in the **same slot**. Force co-location with **hash tags**: only the part inside `{...}` is hashed, so `{user:42}:cart` and `{user:42}:profile` share a slot. Overusing one tag creates hot shards.
- Resharding moves slots between nodes online.
- Cluster mode historically supports only database 0 (`SELECT` is unavailable); Valkey 9 added numbered databases in cluster mode.
- Consistency is not strong: asynchronous replication means acknowledged writes can be lost during failover.

Before sharding, check whether one larger instance (or read replicas) suffices; a single Redis can handle on the order of 100k+ simple operations per second.

lesson.heading: Redis vs Valkey and managed options
lesson.body:
- **Redis** (Redis Ltd.): Redis 8 under RSALv2/SSPLv1/AGPLv3 options, with JSON, search/query, time series, probabilistic structures and vector sets in the core; Redis Cloud and Redis Software for enterprise features (active-active geo replication).
- **Valkey** (Linux Foundation, BSD): fork of Redis 7.2, compatible clients and commands for the core feature set; recent releases focus on performance (improved multi-threaded I/O) and operational features. Default engine for many managed offerings (AWS ElastiCache and MemoryDB for Valkey, Google Memorystore for Valkey) and often cheaper there.
- Other compatible engines: Dragonfly, KeyDB, and serverless HTTP-based Redis APIs such as Upstash for edge and serverless functions.

Choose based on licence requirements, needed modules (search/vector), managed service availability and cost. Application code using standard commands usually runs on either.

keyPoints: RDB: periodic forked snapshots, compact and fast to load, loses recent writes on crash.
AOF with appendfsync everysec loses about a second at most; combine with RDB preamble.
Replication is asynchronous: replica reads can be stale and failover can lose acknowledged writes.
Sentinel (3+ instances, quorum) gives automatic failover and primary discovery without sharding.
Cluster shards 16,384 hash slots across primaries; clients follow MOVED and ASK.
Multi-key operations in Cluster need one slot; use hash tags like {user:42}.
Valkey is the BSD fork offered by major clouds; Redis 8 bundles JSON, search and vector features.

questions.prompt: Which persistence setting loses at most about one second of writes in a crash, with good performance?
questions.explanation: everysec fsyncs the AOF once per second in the background, the usual balance. always is safer but much slower; no depends on the OS flushing (often 30 s).

questions.prompt: A client writes to the primary, gets OK, and the primary crashes before replicating. A replica is promoted. What happens to that write?
options: It is guaranteed to exist on the new primary
It can be lost, because replication is asynchronous
The client receives an error retroactively
questions.explanation: Acknowledgement happens before replication. WAIT reduces the window but Redis does not provide strong consistency guarantees in failover.

questions.prompt: How many hash slots does Redis Cluster use?
questions.explanation: The key space is divided into 16,384 slots, assigned to primaries. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384.

questions.prompt: Which pair of keys is guaranteed to be in the same Cluster slot?
questions.explanation: Only the substring inside the first {...} is hashed when a hash tag is present, so both keys hash "user:42" and land in the same slot. Without tags, similar-looking keys usually hash differently.

questions.prompt: What does Redis Sentinel provide?
options: Monitoring, automatic failover and primary discovery for a primary/replica setup
questions.explanation: Sentinel handles HA for a non-sharded deployment. Redis Cluster provides sharding with built-in failover.

questions.prompt: A client sends GET to a Cluster node that does not own the key's slot. What does it receive?
options: A MOVED error with the slot and the correct node's address
questions.explanation: Nodes do not proxy. The client follows the MOVED redirect and updates its slot map. ASK is returned during slot migration for a one-off redirect.

questions.prompt: Running Redis with AOF persistence makes separate off-host backups unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Persistence protects against process restarts, not against disk loss, accidental FLUSHALL, corruption or region failure. Ship RDB snapshots to other storage.

questions.prompt: Redis Sentinel should run with at least three instances on independent machines.
questions.explanation: A quorum among independent Sentinels avoids false failovers and keeps failover possible when one Sentinel or host is down.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which statements about Redis Cluster are true?
options: Multi-key commands require all keys in the same hash slot
It supports SELECT with numbered databases in classic Redis Cluster
Clients must handle MOVED and ASK redirections
Each shard can have replicas for failover
questions.explanation: Same-slot multi-key operations, redirect handling and per-shard replicas are core features. Classic Redis Cluster only supports database 0, and replication is asynchronous, so writes are not strongly consistent.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the AOF option appendfsync ___ fsyncs once per second and is the default.
questions.explanation: everysec bounds data loss to roughly one second while keeping throughput high.

questions.prompt: Explain Redis persistence options and how you would configure them for a cache vs a session store.
questions.answer:
- RDB: point-in-time snapshots via fork; compact, fast restart, good backups; loses changes since last snapshot; fork cost on big datasets.
- AOF: log of writes; everysec loses about 1 s; rewrites compact it; larger files and slower restarts than RDB, mitigated by the RDB preamble.
- Cache: persistence often off (or RDB only for warm restarts); losing data is acceptable; eviction policy allkeys-lru/lfu.
- Session store: AOF everysec plus RDB snapshots shipped off-host, replication with automatic failover (Sentinel or managed), noeviction or volatile policy, memory alerts.
- Queues (BullMQ): like sessions, plus monitoring of memory and fsync latency.

questions.prompt: Sentinel vs Cluster: when do you need each?
questions.answer:
- Sentinel: one primary with replicas, automatic failover and service discovery. Use when the dataset and write load fit on one node and you need HA. Simple client semantics: all keys on one node, multi-key operations unrestricted.
- Cluster: data sharded across many primaries (16,384 slots), each with replicas and built-in failover. Use when memory or write throughput exceeds a single node. Costs: cluster-aware clients, same-slot requirement for multi-key ops/Lua/transactions (hash tags), hot-shard risk, resharding operations.
- Both use async replication, so failover can lose recent writes. Managed services (ElastiCache/Memorystore for Valkey or Redis, Redis Cloud) handle most of this operationally.

questions.prompt: Your company runs Redis on AWS. Would you choose Redis or Valkey, and why?
questions.answer:
For standard use (caching, sessions, rate limiting, BullMQ, pub/sub, streams) both are command- and client-compatible, so the choice is mostly cost, licence and features.
- Valkey: BSD licence, Linux Foundation governance with broad vendor backing, offered as the default and typically cheaper engine on ElastiCache/MemoryDB, active performance work.
- Redis 8: if you need its built-in Query Engine (search, secondary indexing), JSON, time series or vector sets, or Redis Enterprise features (active-active), via Redis Cloud or self-managed under its licences.
I would default to managed Valkey for core workloads, keep code on standard commands and well-supported clients (ioredis/node-redis or valkey-glide), and choose Redis where its modules are a real requirement.
